node.label: Darlene Clark Hine
node.description: Historian of Black women, work and professional institutions. In her 1989 essay Hine argued that migration and institutional histories require attention to sexual violence and a protective culture of dissemblance, while acknowledging limits in this explanation. Celia J. Wintz reads Black Women in White (1989) as a revisionist nursing history centered on racial and gender barriers. Hine’s 2003 opening meta-argument places parallel Black professional organizations within the conditions of resistance to white supremacy. These are distinct historical explanations, rather than an assertion that all Black women shared one experience or method.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Black Women in White: Racial Conflict and Cooperation in the Nursing Profession, 1890–1950 (1989); “Rape and the Inner Lives of Black Women in the Middle West” (1989; earlier conference version 1988); “Black Professionals and Race Consciousness” (published 2003). Reader: Celia J. Wintz (1991).

proposed_edges.relationship: The culture of dissemblance: sexual violence, privacy and Black women’s migration require analytical explanation beyond the recovery of prominent lives (1989).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own essay, pp.912–916 and 919–920 read. Hine treats sexual/personal motives as additions to economic explanations and acknowledges that dissemblance can be mistaken for control over hostile representations. Her historical generalizations are not universal findings for all Black women.

proposed_edges.relationship: Black Women in White (1989) studies Black nurses’ struggles against racial and gender exclusion; Hine’s later argument makes parallel professional organizations important to resistance (2003).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The nursing-book interpretation is attributed to Celia J. Wintz’s read repository abstract; the book is not newly read. Hine’s 2003 published opening extract, rather than the whole address, supplies the parallel-institutions argument. A scoped contribution to nursing/professional history, not founding medical history.
